source: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving, Memory & Cognition 15(3)
finding: Founding study. Solvers rated warmth (0-10) every 10 s (15 s in Exp 2). Insight problems showed a sudden jump from cold to solved. Multi-step problems showed gradual warmth before the answer. Warmth predicted success only for multi-step problems.
numbers: 73 subjects, only 39 gave usable data (as reported in a search summary and Hedne 2016). Ratings every 10 s; solvers had to be 100% sure before answering; up to 40 ratings per problem.
limits: Paywalled, not opened; known only through later papers. Insight defined by problem type, not by solver experience. Small usable sample.
agent_relevance: Basis for the claim that gradual warmth is a signal for step-wise problems only. A progress trigger may work on incremental tasks and fail on insight-type tasks.

source: Hedne, Norman & Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
finding: Failed to replicate the warmth difference between insight and noninsight solutions. Insight was self-labelled, not problem-typed.
numbers: N=51, 32 magic-trick videos of 15 s, 971 trials kept. Differential warmth: insight M=2.92 vs noninsight M=0.30, t(210)=0.79, p=.429, d=0.12. Angular warmth p=.266, d=0.22. Only trials with 3-4 ratings used, about 70% of trials dropped.
quote: There was no difference between the two types of solution in warmth ratings
limits: Warmth data sparse. Max 5 ratings, low-confidence answers allowed, unlike the 1987 design. Authors say result does not settle sudden vs gradual.
agent_relevance: A warmth-style signal does not reliably separate solvable-soon from stuck states when measured sparsely. Do not rely on one self-rating.

source: Hedne et al. (2016) same paper, confidence and accuracy results
finding: Insight solutions were more accurate and held with more confidence, but confidence tracked accuracy only for noninsight solutions.
numbers: Accuracy insight .57 vs noninsight .37, t(506.9)=5.78, d=0.51. Confidence 78.3 vs 69.0, d=0.50. Type-2 AUC: insight 0.56 (not above chance, p=.142), noninsight 0.63 (above chance, d=0.82), 33 participants.
limits: Self-reported insight label; magic tricks only.
agent_relevance: Self-reported confidence can be unreliable exactly on the hard, restructuring-type items. Matches the schema note that the model's own stuck signal is weak (r=.17).

source: Hedne et al. (2016) same paper, solution time
finding: Solution times did not clearly differ between insight and noninsight.
numbers: Insight M=38.23 s vs noninsight 40.56 s, t(969)=1.705, p=.089, d=0.10 (units as reported by the page summary; videos were 15 s, so check against the paper).
limits: Unit oddity unresolved.
agent_relevance: Time spent alone is a weak cue for which mode of solving is happening.

source: Kizilirmak, Serger, Kehl, Ollinger, Folta-Schoofs & Richardson-Klavehn (2018) Feelings-of-warmth increase more abruptly for verbal riddles solved with in contrast to without Aha!
finding: Partial support for Metcalfe & Wiebe when insight is defined by the solver's Aha! report. Warmth rose more steeply in the last two ratings before Aha! solutions.
numbers: N=36, 90 Compound Remote Associates items, 30 s each, 5-point warmth rated every 5-6 s. Last minus third-to-last warmth: 2.59 (SD 0.97) with Aha! vs 1.43 (SD 1.07) without, t(26)=4.27, p<.001, d=0.82. Round x Aha interaction F(2,52)=15.63, np2=.375. Aha! in 76% of generated vs 57% of non-generated solutions (p=.016).
limits: 27 solved items for the test. Only 20, 13, 9 people for longer curves. Rating may interrupt solving. Unsolved items: warmth stayed 0-1, no Aha/no-Aha difference (p=.207).
agent_relevance: Progress feeling is graded for ordinary solves and steeper for sudden ones. Warmth on unsolved items stays flat, so flat low progress does mark failure.

source: Laukkonen & Tangen (2018) How to detect insight moments in problem solving experiments, Frontiers in Psychology 9:282
finding: Warmth-defined insight and self-reported insight agree across people but barely agree item by item.
numbers: N=80, 20 verbal insight problems, 180 solved problems with 2+ warmth ratings. Participant level r=.61 (self-report M=5.28 vs warmth M=4.85 per person). Problem level r=.08, p=.235, n=182. When warmth showed sudden solution, 75.6% were self-reported insight; when gradual, still 50.8%.
limits: Warmth every 10 s gave few ratings on fast solves. Only correct solves. No ground truth for insight.
agent_relevance: Warmth curves are a noisy item-level indicator. A trigger built on a single curve would misfire on many items.

source: Laukkonen & Tangen (2018) proposed measure
finding: Proposes differential warmth (needs only two ratings) as a cheaper insight measure and a dynamometer grip measure, untested here.
numbers: Warmth data available for 180 of 631 solved problems.
limits: Dynamometer is a proposal only.
agent_relevance: A two-point change is cheaper than a full curve; the same idea as comparing the last two checks.

source: Graf, Danek, Vaci & Bilalic (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving using GAMs and change point analysis, J. Intelligence 11(5):86
finding: Re-analysis of eye tracking on a matchstick problem. Attention to the key operator jumped just before the solution for solvers (change point near the 90% time bin). After a hint, solvers showed gradual attention growth.
numbers: N=61. 34% solved before the hint, 11% more after. GAM and change-point methods agree on the late jump for solvers. Dwell time on the plus sign about doubled after the hint for non-solvers.
limits: Footnote says plotted data were simulated to show a sudden shift; original shift was gradual. One problem. No warmth data.
agent_relevance: Behaviour can change abruptly just before success, so late signals exist but come too late to be a trigger.

source: Moroshkina et al. (2024) The Aha! experience is associated with a drop in the perceived difficulty of the problem, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Stronger Aha! goes with a larger drop in rated difficulty between early and post-solution ratings. Supports a difficulty re-appraisal view of progress.
numbers: N=160 (164 recruited), 55 Russian rebus puzzles, 25 s limit, difficulty rated at about 5 s and after solving. Correct solutions: beta=0.18, SE=0.04, p<.001. Incorrect solutions: beta=0.03, p=.734. Unsolved with answer shown: beta=0.05, p=.012.
limits: Difficulty rated only at two points. No warmth or solvability judgments. Single 7-point Aha item.
agent_relevance: Early difficulty estimates change after success, so an early difficulty rating is a prior, not a progress meter.

source: Wiley & Miller (2026) Aha! ratings as metacognitive judgments, J. Intelligence 14(9):198
finding: Aha! ratings are tied to getting the right answer, not to restructuring. Highest after a correct first move.
numbers: N=377, 4 spatial problems, 1,164 observations. Aha vs correctness F(1,1091)=112.17, R2partial=.09, f2=0.099. Mindset not linked to solution rate (B=-0.04, p=.632).
limits: Four problems, 68% female, single-item rating, correlational. Warmth not collected.
agent_relevance: Subjective feeling of insight mostly reflects result and fluency cues. Agents should not treat a felt-progress token as evidence.

source: Ishikawa, Toshima & Mogi (2019) How and when? Metacognition and solution timing characterize an Aha experience of object recognition in hidden figures, Frontiers in Psychology 10:1023
finding: Aha experiences in object recognition came with higher accuracy and confidence, and confidence discriminated correct from incorrect answers well.
numbers: N=10, 650 trials, 95.2% recognised, 89.2% of those correct. Aha-rated insight solutions 98.2% vs 89.8% correct, t(9)=2.81, p=.02. Type-2 AUC 0.90 (95% CI 0.81-0.98). Aha vs suddenness rs=.78.
limits: N=10, exploratory, confidence at ceiling (48.5% maximum), only 39 errors. No warmth measure.
agent_relevance: Post-hoc confidence can be well calibrated on perception tasks, unlike mid-solving progress. Use confidence at answer time, not as an in-process trigger.

source: Ollinger, Fedor, Brodt & Szathmary (2016/2017) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization, Psychological Research
finding: A hint to maximise line intersections solved the problem; hints on lines or intersections alone did not. Supports heuristic-guided search plus constraint relaxation, using MacGregor's maximization heuristic.
numbers: N=120 (116 analysed). Solved: control 10% (3/30), line 7%, intersection 21%, maximization 72% (21/29). Maximization vs control chi2(1,59)=23.80, p<.0001, phi=.64. Solvers had fewer attempts (8.41 vs 10.93, d=.62) and more variation (.59 vs .43, d=.67). Logistic model 87.8% correct, Nagelkerke R2=.61.
quote: relaxing constraints was necessary but not sufficient to solve the problem
limits: Maximization group received all three hints (confounded). Progress monitoring and look-ahead not measured directly. Authors do not name a criterion of satisfaction.
agent_relevance: A well-chosen progress criterion (what to maximise) can lift solve rate far above a bare no-progress check. The criterion matters more than the trigger.

source: Spiridonov, Loginov, Ivanchei & Kurgansky (2019) The role of motor activity in insight problem solving (nine-dot), Frontiers in Psychology 10:2
finding: Nine-dot problem: motor training that breaks the dot-turn habit raised solving. Solvers were slower and paused more late on, read as look-ahead planning. Authors say neither progress-monitoring nor representational change theory predicts motor effects.
numbers: Exp1 N=36, solve rate 52.8%. Exp2 N=64: 78.1% with non-dot-turn training vs 37.5% with dot-turn training, chi2(1)=10.83, p=.001. Solvers' stage-3 speed t(50)=6.07, d=1.49. Exp3 N=58, implicit sequence training no significant effect (24.1% vs 48.3%, p=.101).
limits: Small, mostly female, one problem, insight not verified. Progress monitoring not tested directly. MacGregor model lookahead of 1-4 line segments is cited, not tested.
agent_relevance: Lookahead depth is a lever separate from the stuck trigger. Pauses (thinking time) before action predicted success.

source: Doulfoukar, Pezzulo & Stuyck (2026) Unveiling the Aha! moment: a computational account of insight in active inference, Psychonomic Bull. & Rev.
finding: Model where insight is a Bayesian model reduction step. Predicts a sharp confidence jump at restructuring and a gradual rise without it. Does not model warmth or progress monitoring.
numbers: 60 simulated agents (30 BMR, 30 non-BMR). BMR agent insight at trial 25/26, non-BMR inferred rule at trial 33. Confidence drop at inferred insight 1.22 bits (humans, Ollinger et al. 2023 data) vs 1.43 bits (BMR agents).
limits: Rule built in, one task, parameters tuned for speed, human insight moment is a proxy, a figure caption conflicts with the text.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal reason progress signals can be flat then jump: model change, not drift. Argues for a restructuring operator, not a longer search.

source: 2021 review: Current understanding of the insight phenomenon across disciplines, Frontiers in Psychology 12:791398
finding: States that progress monitoring theory (MacGregor et al. 2001; Chu et al. 2007) treats insight as conscious search with abandonment of failing assumptions; the rival is representational change (unconscious). Names no experiment that separates them and gives no numbers for progress monitoring.
numbers: No quantitative results for these topics.
limits: Page read to 100k of 121k characters. Warmth not mentioned. Replication status not discussed.
agent_relevance: No decisive experiment separating the theories is described. Treat the trigger rule as an engineering choice, not a settled psychological fact.

source: Friedlander & Fine (2018) The penny drops: investigating insight through cryptic crosswords, Frontiers in Psychology 9:904
finding: Survey of cryptic crossword solvers. Setting a puzzle aside helps, and Aha! is strongest after long struggle. No solving-trajectory data.
numbers: Survey N=805. 94.6% say putting the puzzle aside helps; 80.3% say the answer is often obvious on return; 79.6% say Aha is most intense after a long struggle. Trial: 682 of 756 clues solved (90.2%), 28 solvers, think-aloud not yet analysed.
limits: Self-report, trial unpublished, English-speaking culture only.
agent_relevance: Supports a reset or incubation step after a stall. No progress-curve evidence.

source: Metacognitive bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal fundamental limits of machine insight and self-evaluation in reasoning AI (arXiv 2509.14704, v3 2026)
finding: 38 frontier LLMs on insight-like riddles fall far below humans. Models often write the correct answer in their reasoning but do not choose it as final (verification failure).
numbers: 201 riddles, 120-item human subset, human n=126, mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6-59.2). Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%. GPT-5 inside human CI. Verification failures were 5.23% (Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview) to 39.34% (Grok 4) of incorrect answers; DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57%, Claude Opus 4 25.00%.
quote: models generate a correct intermediate candidate but fail to endorse it as their final answer
limits: Table 2 uses literal string match in thought logs; only four models with usable logs; observational; GPT-5 overlap is not equivalence.
agent_relevance: Strong case for a code-level check that scores candidates found mid-trace. Progress is sometimes made and then lost; keep best-so-far.

source: Nazonazo paper, false insight observation
finding: Some thought logs show confident commitment to a wrong reinterpretation, compared with human false insight. Described as analogy only.
numbers: Qualitative; no rate given.
limits: Descriptive, no count.
agent_relevance: High felt progress can be wrong. Progress signals need an external check.

source: Yan et al. (2026) UPAIR: Diagnosing reasoning states via uncertainty-progress alignment for selective intervention (arXiv 2607.17188)
finding: Training-free monitor combining answer uncertainty (entropy from a small proxy model) and a hidden-state progress measure. Diagnoses healthy, stagnant or ready states and acts: continue, switch strategy, or stop.
numbers: 3 models (Qwen3-8B, R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, QwQ-32B) x 5 benchmarks. Higher accuracy in all 15 settings, fewer tokens in 10. Stagnation flag catches 64.3% of natural errors and flags 5.4% of correct samples; 80.3% of flagged samples are wrong. Best gain QwQ-32B AIME 2025 +16.67 pts. MATH-500 tokens -29.6%.
limits: No limitations section. LiveCodeBench gains small (+1.2 to +1.8). Larger proxy did not help (1.5B best). Needs hidden states. Candidate answer set must be built per task. AIME sets are 30 problems, so one-problem swings are 3.3 pts.
agent_relevance: Closest AI analogue of a graded progress rule. Joint signal beat uncertainty alone (flagged pool 91.67% errors vs 73.33% on AIME 2025, R1-14B). Strategy switch drove all gains.

source: UPAIR baselines table (CUSUM, Tracing, DEER, DynaSteer, CyclicReflex, Think-or-Not)
finding: Single-signal stopping and steering baselines were inconsistent: several were below vanilla on some benchmarks.
numbers: Qwen3-8B AIME 2024 vanilla 72.22; DEER 70.00; Think-or-Not 68.89; CyclicReflex 65.55; UPAIR 77.78. LiveCodeBench vanilla 41.92; DEER 38.32; UPAIR 43.11. QwQ-32B AIME 2025 CyclicReflex 40.00 vs vanilla 50.00.
limits: Authors' own runs. Small AIME samples.
agent_relevance: A hard single trigger can hurt. Early stop or reflection-penalty rules lost accuracy on code and AIME in several settings.

source: UPAIR mechanism example and runtime
finding: On 30 AIME 2025 samples with QwQ-32B, UPAIR corrected 5 wrong to right with 0 right to wrong; CyclicReflex moved 2 wrong to right and 5 right to wrong. Monitoring costs under 1% of time.
numbers: Vanilla 15/30, CyclicReflex 12/30, UPAIR 20/30. Proxy monitoring 1.44 s, geometry 0.78 s per sample vs target decoding 252.81 s (0.88% overhead). End-to-end 255.02 s vs 292.06 s.
limits: 30 problems, one model. Overhead excludes proxy hosting cost.
agent_relevance: Intervening only on a diagnosed stall avoids harming correct runs; that is the property to copy.

source: Hosseini et al. (2026) Early stopping for large reasoning models via confidence dynamics, CoDE-Stop (arXiv 2604.04930)
finding: Tracks confidence of intermediate answers; correct runs reach high confidence early, incorrect runs wander. Stops on high confidence or on a degeneration score. Saves cost with some accuracy loss.
numbers: Budget 32768, mean of AIME24/25, MATH500, GSM8K, GPQA-D. Qwen3-4B 78.4 to 76.9 acc, cost 8344 to 5960 (-28.6%). Qwen3-14B 83.3 to 78.1, cost -43.1%. R1-Distill-Llama-8B 66.0 to 63.3, -22.2%. Nemotron-8B 73.2 to 71.3, -19.3%.
limits: Accuracy fell 1.5 to 5.2 points. Versus DEER only 4-9% cheaper and accuracy not consistently better. Gains smaller at 16K budget. Threshold tuned on AMC23. Abstract says 25-50% but table gives 19-43%.
agent_relevance: Confidence trend is a usable stop signal but trades accuracy for tokens. It fits a stop rule, not an escape rule.

source: CoDE-Stop ablations
finding: A trend-aware indicator (confidence below twice the previous minus the one before, delta 0.55) worked best; log weighting favouring earlier steps worked best; normalising weights removed most savings.
numbers: Stop threshold ramps 0.9 to 0.95; steps split at Wait tokens; Alternatively gave similar results. Answer Convergence baseline accuracy about 20-30% overall.
limits: Open models only, 4 benchmarks, few rollouts (1 for GSM8K).
agent_relevance: Graded and trend-based beats raw-level thresholds, in line with the gradual-monitoring human findings.

source: Li et al. (2026) Stop when further reasoning won't help: attention-state adaptive generation, ASAG (arXiv 2606.15070, ICML 2026 Spotlight)
finding: Training-free early stop from attention patterns; abstract reports small accuracy gain with big token savings.
numbers: Abstract: +3.2% average accuracy, nearly 40% fewer tokens on Qwen3-8B, 9 benchmarks, DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Qwen3 series.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Signal details and baselines not read.
agent_relevance: Another internal-state progress signal; needs model internals our scaffold may not have.

source: Early-exit family (LYNX, PUMA, STACK, ReCo) from arXiv search listing
finding: Many 2025-2026 methods cut reasoning tokens with progress or convergence signals. Reported cuts: LYNX 35-70% (probe plus conformal prediction), PUMA about 26% (semantic redundancy), STACK 59.9% on math, ReCo 37-65%.
limits: Listing only; not opened; no accuracy numbers read.
agent_relevance: The field converges on stop rules. Escape-when-stuck rules are less studied than stop-when-done rules.

source: Hedne et al. (2016) account of method differences from Metcalfe & Wiebe
finding: Authors name design differences as the likely cause of the failed replication: 100% confidence required before answering and up to 40 warmth ratings per problem in 1987, versus low-confidence answers and at most 5 ratings in 2016.
numbers: 40 vs 5 ratings per problem; 100% confidence vs free answering.
limits: Explanation untested.
agent_relevance: Progress measures depend on how often they are sampled. A count-based code rule samples every step and avoids this.

source: Kizilirmak et al. (2018) unsolved items and difficulty
finding: On unsolved items warmth stayed low and Aha status made no difference. Item difficulty did not change Aha! rates.
numbers: Unsolved n=34; warmth between 0 and 1; Aha vs no-Aha p=.207. Difficulty effect on Aha p=.197.
limits: Few trials per curve.
agent_relevance: Persistently low rated progress is a genuine fail signal in this task.
